stories.title_ja: Claude Fable 5.1 と Claude Mythos 5.1

comments.author: felixrieseberg
comments.text: (I work at Anthropic) Beyond all the benchmarks, I think Fable 5.1 is a big improvement in writing style. It sounds a lot less stereotypically like other Claude models, has (imho) a much more natural style, and responds to my style instructions more reliably. More work to be done (and we will!) but reading better prose makes me so much happier. Another point I expect not to get much attention until it all happens at once is science. People have been correctly excited about the many "sudden" breakthroughs LLMs are making in Maths, but some of the science benchmarks make me believe we'll soon see similar developments in other scientific domains. Fable 5.1 more than doubled Fable 5's Terminal-Bench-Science [1] score, which I think is meaningful. [1] https://github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench-science

comments.author: simonw
comments.text: Pelicans for thinking effort low, medium, high and xhigh (that xhigh one is pretty good): https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer#url=ht... I'm still waiting for effort max to finish. EDIT: I fixed a bug in my tooling so it now records summarized reasoning traces - here's that max pelican, which is a significant improvement: https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer#url=ht... Took just under 14 minutes to generate, and at 65927 output tokens cost me a hefty $3.30! Excerpts from the reasoning trace: > Adding pedal shapes near both feet, with the far foot on the second leg partially visible behind the frame. I'm considering whether to add a small scarf or cap for extra character, but leaning toward keeping it simple to avoid clutter. > Now I'm debating a bicycle helmet on the head versus the pelican's signature crest—the beak and pouch already read clearly as "pelican," so a helmet could reinforce the bicycle theme without losing identity, though it might compete with the crest for visual space. > I realize the beak at (484,84) would overlap with the dome helmet, so I need to shrink the helmet so it only covers the top of the head, adjusting its arc endpoints to sit higher and narrower so the beak can attach cleanly at the front without collision. [...] > I'm adding a darker tip region to represent the primary feathers, then reconsidering the trailing edge to include scalloped feather curves instead of one smooth line for a more natural look. [...] > Now I'm checking the vent line placements on the helmet, making sure they sit far enough inside the helmet's edge given the stroke width and rounded caps, and confirming each vent stays within the helmet's circular boundary. [...] > I decide skipping a handlebar bell and tire highlights since they're unnecessary additions. Now I'm reconsidering the front fork's curve — the current control point pulls the shape backward when it should bow forward for a proper rake, so I need to shift the control point rightward to fix the fork's lean. This is a notable result because most of the recent Claude models have been pretty bad at drawing pelicans, at least when compared to models in the Gemini or GLM series.

comments.author: GodelNumbering
comments.text: The price reduction comes from the cache read pricing falling from $1/M to $0.25/M, which means that Fable 5.1 now costs half of Opus's cache read costs ($0.5/M). This gives a lot of credit to the theory that Anthropic did not get much bite on Fable at its original pricing, which in turn likely places a ceiling on LLM pricing in general. Interestingly also, if you take away terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 results, it is hard to see ANY improvement: Terminal-Bench 4.0: Fable 5.1 is +3.5% vs Opus 5. GDPval-AA v2: +1.5% vs Opus 5. OSWorld 2.0: +2.5% vs Opus 5. Humanity's Last Exam (with tools): +1.6% Keep in mind that this is supposed to be an entirely higher tier of a model than Opus 5. For one tier up and one version up, these are not really improvements. Probably leaves no room to place Opus 5.1 anywhere. Combined with the fact that they are selling 'readability'... Has frontier progress finally stalled?

comments.author: mlaux
comments.text: Looks like all three breaking changes are patches for inadvertent chain of thought disclosure. Someone found out (don't have the tweet handy) that if you created a bogus "think_deeply" tool and then forced the model to use it, it would output what is believed to be its raw thinking there - I believe the first breaking change stops this. The second two are aimed at people getting Haiku to repeat thinking blocks from other models verbatim (since it can see the decrypted version). I get that in their eyes it's an "exploit" but still kinda disappointing that they patched this

comments.author: madrox
comments.text: I am finding that I am now less interested in better models than I am in token budgets. My issue with Anthropic models now is that I don't feel like I can rely on them as a daily driver because they'll dry up before my quota resets. I am becoming dependent on AI to make a living, and I need predictable spend on it. If I know I can't use a model regularly all month, my enthusiasm is limited. I urge Anthropic to get better at this aspect of their business so I can come back to it.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、Claude Fable 5.1の文章スタイルの向上と科学ベンチマークでのスコア改善、そして価格設定とトークン予算への懸念、さらに思考過程の漏洩を防ぐパッチについてである。賛否では、スタイルが自然になり指示に従いやすくなったことや、Terminal‑Bench‑Scienceスコアが約2倍になった点が肯定的に評価される一方で、他のベンチマークではOpus 5との差がわずかで、段階上位のモデルとしては物足りないという批判がある。価格面ではキャッシュ読み取りコストが半減しコストパフォーマンスが改善されたが、これが価格の上限を示し、今後の値上げ余地が少ないと指摘されている。また、トークン予算の予測不能さが日常利用の障壁になるという声もある。注目コメントとして、Anthropic社員は文体の自然さと科学分野での将来的 breakthrough を期待し、別のユーザーは pelican の描画過程を詳細に追える理由付けトレースを示し、思考量に応じた出力コスト（約14分で65927トークン、3.30ドル）を具体的に示した点が洞察に富んでいる。
stories.editor_note: Claude Fable 5.1 と Claude Mythos 5.1 は、物語創作や神話生成に特化した言語モデルで、日本のゲームやアニメ制作におけるAI活用の具体例として注目されている。

stories.title_en: Hang on to Your Firefox
stories.title_ja: Firefoxを離さないで

comments.author: autoexec
comments.text: > Meanwhile, the over thinkers on Hacker News come up with convoluted reasons to hate on Firefox every time the subject arises...Firefox is our last best hope for browser engine diversity and competition. It's exactly because Firefox is so important that you'll see people here complaining when Firefox does things to push away users like Mozilla buying up an ad-tech company, collecting data on users, and using firefox to push personalized ads, or the addition of anti-features and questionable design choices that force us to hunt for and modify poorly documented settings in about:config and make edits to userChrome.css It isn't bots complaining about Firefox here, it's power users who are frustrated by what Firefox is turning into. Users who are seriously concerned about what Mozilla is prioritizing, and who are genuinely worried about what is at stake. I hope people here never stop bitching about Firefox. Refusing to talk about Firefox's problems wont help make them go away. Keep discussing what you'd like to see in Firefox and what things you hope they'll focus on and prioritize. There are Firefox devs and mozilla employees around here. If we're lucky, a few of them might see and listen to some of what we say. It's the most tech savvy users who disable all the telemetry and data collection, so our feedback isn't really going to be seen any other way.

comments.author: roughly
comments.text: There’s an old mantra from organizing: “no permanent enemies, no permanent allies.” You will never align with another group or person 100% on all things; the secret to making change is to build a coalition of those with whom you agree on an issue without holding it against them that you disagree on a different one. I disagree with Mozilla about many things, but I agree with this article - I use Firefox because it’s the only browser out there that isn’t Chrome or WebKit, and that’s worth enough to me that I’m willing to disagree with them on other issues.

comments.author: hx8
comments.text: I am under the impression that Firefox is the only web browser which has access to quality ad blocker. Am I incorrect in this? How is this not enough of a selling point for everyone to switch to it?

comments.author: Nail2680
comments.text: Firefox is the best of a bunch of bad options, but isn't above critique. It does suck when they do anticonsumer stuff and shove weird stuff like pocket in, but you can't leave which makes it similar to the democratic party where you can't really do anything, but they keep making really poor decisions.

comments.author: throwlifeaway
comments.text: Part of the blame for what's wrong with the web right now is on web developers: - We "need" firefox or else everything's just chrome - Forks of chrome don't count as different browsers because they all use the same engine - Using the same engine makes you basically just chrome because you can't diverge from upstream - You can't diverge from upstream because it moves too fast and you need to keep merging with it - You need to keep merging with upstream because upstream is implementing new web platform features - You need those web platform features because if you don't add them then websites will stop working in your fork - Websites will stop working in your fork because web developers don't support older browser versions - Web developers don't support older browser versions because... they don't care? If web developers had a culture of supporting, say, 10 years of previous browser versions, then chromium would lose a lot of the power it has to drag the forks (and firefox) behind it. I don't really see this happening without some sort of major culture shift, though. Maybe if we had some versioned web standard that lagged behind the "real" ones so sites could say "StableWeb 2.0 Compatible!" or something.

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点  
Firef ​​oxのブラウザエンジンの多様性確保が重要である一方、Mozillaの広告技術関連企買、ユーザーデータ収集、パーソナル広告導入などに対する批判が活発に行われている。これらの問題は自動botによるのではなく、高度な技術知識を持つユーザー、特にテレメトリーを無効化しているパワーユーザーからの苦情であると指摑される。

・賛否両論  
Firefoxを支持する意見では、ChromeやWebKit以外の選択肩を維持すること自体が重要であり、Mozillaとの差異を指摘しつつもその存在を肯定する立場がある。一方、批判する意見では、アンチフィーチャーや設計選択、about:configやuserChrome.cssの非文書化されたカスタマイズ要求などによりユーザー体験が悪化しているとの見解が対立している。

・注目コメント  
「組織論における格言『永久の敵も永久の同盟者もない』ように、Mozillaとの意見の違いを超えてFirefoxの存在そのものを支持すべきだ」というコメントが的確に両論を融合させる視点として注目されている。また、Web開発者文化が新しいブラウザエンジンの分散を阻んでおり、長期的なブラウザサポート文化の確立がウェブの多様性回復につながるとの分析も話題を集めている。
stories.editor_note: Firefoxを離さないで は、プライバシー重視のブラウザとしてのFirefoxの価値を再確認させ、欧州の規制強化と日本の個人情報保護法改正との関連が話題になっている。

stories.title_en: How accurate have Ed Zitron's AI skeptic predictions been?
stories.title_ja: Ed ZitronのAI懐疑的予測はどれほど正確か？

comments.author: solid_fuel
comments.text: I would be interested in seeing a similar list of predictions from Altman, Amodei, etc with annotations about how many have come true. Ed Zitron is a blow hard and frequently overstates things to the point where it is hard to take seriously, but so are the AI industry leaders. I have heard multiple breathless press releases warning that the end of white collar work is "just 6 months away" and that people not using the latest Mythos/Fable/Whatever model will be hopelessly left behind.

comments.author: pcstl
comments.text: Zitron has become the distorted reflection of the very AI boosters he criticizes and mocks. I think the worst thing that happened to him was AI skepticism becoming a political position . This gave him a captive audience - as long as he says what they want to hear , which means that he can never ever concede that he might have been wrong or that AI might actually be progressing or having successes. This is not conducive to good prediction long-term - rather it leads one to a state of cognitive dissonance where one's chosen enemies must be simultaneously terrifyingly powerful and incompetent dunces. The propagandist's disease.

comments.author: achompas
comments.text: One thing I’m observing in these comments is a willingness of folks to project their own predictions onto Ed’s statements when validating their plausibility. Eg. “I think he’s wrong about the timing but I do expect AI companies to go to zero.” You can do that, but then you’re no longer discussing his predictions. You’re discussing your predictions, and your own positioning. Those differ from Dan’s essay, which engages with the literal text of Ed’s numerous predictions during 2024 and 2025 which are demonstrably invalidated by their measurable outcomes.

comments.author: jsrozner
comments.text: Though the bubble has not popped, I don't see the following discussed in the post: Zitron would probably point out (as have others) that many of the hyperscalers are booking valuation increases in Anthropic, OpenAI as "Other Income", which is substantially increasing their reported revenue and earnings. It's roughly: - Hyperscalers like Goog, Meta, Msft invest cash in Anthropic, OpenAI, in exchange for equity - The ongoing investment actually boosts the valuations in the Anthr/OpenAI (new raises are done at higher valuations), so the valuation of the Hyperscaler's existing investments in Anthr/OpenAI increases, which gets recorded as Other Income in quarterly earnings - Much of that invested cash will itself come back (circularly) to the hyperscalers as revenue since Anthropic and OpenAI spend a lot of money via datacenters etc. On Other Income phenomenon, see for example, https://www.ft.com/content/be97df0a-76b1-4cb0-9ba4-d1117d8d1... Also, there's apparently lots of off-balance sheet debt. For example https://www.ft.com/content/a0a07cce-6d19-4b1e-a73b-9855a06ba...

comments.author: sfblah
comments.text: I don't think Zitron is wrong, exactly. He's just early. There are a lot of analysts who have faced the same criticism over the past 10-15 years. IMO the issue is that they fail to understand the staggering size and scope of the government fiscal + monetary interventions across those years. Essentially, the government has jammed all the risk into the future to repeatedly rescue near-term results. I think something similar is happening with e.g. Amodei's predictions of mass unemployment due to AI. It won't happen in the immediate term, because deficit spending removes the economic incentive for firms to pare down their workforces. All that said, I don't think these people are "wrong," per se. They're just early. When the sh*t hits the fan on all this, it's going to be a big problem. And, for example, companies whose primary business is collecting money for Internet ads will come face to face with the reality of how low value their products are. I have some insight into this, as I work for such a firm, and I know the true extent of the bot traffic out there.

stories.summary_ja:

stories.title_en: Show HN: Weedout – Safari extension that hides YouTube AI-labeled videos
stories.title_ja: Show HN: Weedout – YouTubeのAIラベル付き動画を隠すSafari拡張機能

comments.author: lukeasch21
comments.text: This is great, but why start with Safari and not a cross platform browser? Is there something native here that can't be done otherwise or is it just personal preference?

comments.author: thatmf
comments.text: I wish I had this but for every website and media surface

comments.author: singpolyma3
comments.text: I'm more concerned about the stuff that is fraudulent then possibly legit stuff explicitly labelled as AI

comments.author: ranger_danger
comments.text: You can charge money for browser extensions? And people pay for them? I'm in the wrong business.

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
コミュニティの中心的な関心は、この Safari 拡張機能の選択理由と普遍性に対する疑問に集まった。参開者らはなぜ macOS/iOS ユーザーに限定され、他のブラウザや OS に対応しないのかを問い、「Safari にネイティブな機能があるのか、開発者個人の好みなのか」と突っ込んだ。さらに、「YouTube 以外のすべてのメディア表面にもこのフィルタリングを適用できれば」という声が上がり、AI コンテンツフィルタリングの汎用化への期待が示された。

**賛否両論**  
肯否ははっきり対立している。肯定派は「YouTube 上の AI 生成コンテンツを自動的に非表示にできるツールは非常に有用」と評価し、拡張機能の存在価値を称賛した。一方、否定または懐疑派は「有料ブラウザ拡張機能で収益化できるのか」に驚きを示し、「AI ラベルの付いた合法的なコンテンツよりも詐欺的な内容の排除に注力すべき」だとの意見を展します。

**注目コメント**  
「You can charge money for browser extensions? And people pay for them? I'm in the wrong business.」というコメントは、開発者が拡張機能の商用化に成功した事実に対する incredulity を表し、広場の一部に対して拡張機能市場の収益性への関心を喚起した。
stories.editor_note: Show HN: Weedout – YouTubeのAIラベル付き動画を隠すSafari拡張機能 は、AI生成コンテンツへのユーザー不信感を反映し、日本でもラベル義務化論議が高まる中で注目されている。

stories.title_en: AnkiDroid: Google Play no longer allowing Open Collective donation link
stories.title_ja: AnkiDroid: Google PlayがOpen Collectiveの寄付リンクを許可しなくなった

comments.author: amiga386
comments.text: Not Google's first rodeo. They pulled the same move in 2019: https://www.phoronix.com/news/WireGuard-Ejected-Play-Store This is why software should not be subjected to an "app store" type distribution system, where a monopolist retains absolute control of what software can run on your devices, and can capriciously deny distribution to developers for whatever reason it likes.

comments.author: dataflow
comments.text: > Play billing "must not be used in cases where payments include … tax exempt donations" > Note: 501(c)(6) is a tax-exempt status; donations are not tax-deductible for the donor. Google's communications explicitly state "tax-exempt". Isn't it pretty obvious that the problem is the donations aren't tax-exempt, despite the organization being tax-exempt? Your note suggests you already understand this. Logically, the payment processor (who deals with sales taxes rather than income taxes) should worry about the taxability of the transaction rather than the tax status of the recipient, right? > Specifically, your app allows users to contribute donations to an organization that is not tax-exempt. So whoever is writing their email is mixing these two up, but you're reading the policy itself and it is fairly clear-cut what it means for you, right?

comments.author: SigmundurM
comments.text: > Donations are not tax-deductible > Because we are a 501(c)(6), OSC is not a registered 501(c)(3) charity; donations to hosted member projects are not tax-deductible. This is consistent with IRS guidelines — open source donations aren't automatically classified as charitable simply because they are FOSS. > If your project has a clear charitable purpose, a 501(c)(3) fiscal sponsor may be a good fit. - https://docs.oscollective.org/welcome-and-introduction-to-os...

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点：Google PlayがOpen Collectiveへの寄付リンクを禁止したこと。寄付が税控除対象外の501(c)(6)団体へのものであるため、「税免除寄付」に関するポリシー違反と判断された点が争点。これに対し、ポリシーの解釈が税免除団体と寄付の税控除性を混同していると指摘する意見と、プラットフォーム規制の必要性を強調する意見が分かれた。  
賛否両論：支持側は、Googleが明示されたポリシーに従い、不適切な課税処理を防ぐための正当な措置だと主張。反対側は、オープンソースプロジェクトへの支援を阻害し、プラットフォーム独占により開発者に任意の制限を課す危険性があると批判し、代替配布やLinux端末への移行を提案。  
注目コメント：過去にWireGuardが同様に排除された例を挙げ、「アプリストアに依存しない配布が求められる」と指摘したコメントが特に洞察的だったほか、寄付先の税免除状況と控除性の混同を指摘する技術的な解説も注目された。
stories.editor_note: AnkiDroid: Google PlayがOpen Collectiveの寄付リンクを許可しなくなった は、オープンソースプロジェクトの資金調達手段がプラットフォームポリシーにより制約される事例で、日本のフリーソフトコミュニティにも影響が懸念される。

stories.title_en: The ChatGPT/Codex app bundles a full copy of LibreOffice

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
CodexアプリにLibreOfficeがバンドルされていることへの驚きと、それが本当に必要かどうかが中心に議論された。古いXLSなどの互換性問題を解決するためにLOを組み込むという実用的理由と、巨大な依存関係やUIの使い勝手の悪さが批判された点が主に取り上げられた。

**賛否両論**  
- **賛成側**：LOは長年にわたって信頼性が高く、特に古いマイクロソフト文書の読み込みに最適だと指摘。バンドルすれば外部ツールに頼らず確実に処理できるため、開発者側の利便性がある。  
- **否定的側**：アプリ全体のサイズが肥大化し、設定がごちゃごちゃしていることから、バンドルは過剰だと感じる声。代わりに必要時にダウンロードする方が適切だという意見もあり、ドキュメント処理だけのために重いスイートを常に搭載する必要性に疑問が呈された。

**注目コメント**  
「実際に自分も古いXLSファイルを読むためにLOをバンドルしているが、それで全ドキュメント処理に使えるようになった。それ以外に同じくらい確実に読める代替ツールは見つからなかった」というコメントは、バンドルの実務的必然性を具体的に示しており、議論の中で最も洞察に富んだ意見として挙げられた。

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点
M4 Pro Mac Miniを用いたローカルモデルの構築に関する議論において、 community で最も注目されたのは、モデルの性能評価が明示的に言及されていないことへの懸念です。特に、Commenterは、RAMが16GBという低规格のMini-PCで複数のモデルを読み込んでも「性能がひどい」と报告しており、他のユーザーが「許容可能な性能」としている基準が明確ではないと指摘しています。この議論の中心は、ローカルモデルの実用性を語る際に、硬件仕様と実際のパフォーマンスの関係をどう測定するかという問題です。

・賛否両論
意见が分かれているのは、ローカルモデルの「許容可能な性能」の定義です。あるユーザーは特定の硬件で快適に動作する例を示す一方で、 Commenterのように、Spec上は可能でも実際には遅くて実用にならないという経験を報告する者もいます。この差異は、使用するモデルのサイズ、タスクの複雑さ、乃至はOSやアプリケーションの最適化の違いによるところが大きく、一律に比較できないという見方があります。

・注目コメント
特に洞察のあるコメントは、 Commenterの「性能が terrible だ」という具体的な不満です。これは、単なる「遅い」という感想ではなく、硬件の制約がローカルモデルの実用性を著しく制限しているという明確な問題提起です。このコメントは、ローカルAIの普及を考える上で、単なる「可能・不可能」の議論ではなく、実際の使用環境における「実用性」の閾値を問う重要な指摘として community に影響を与えました。
stories.editor_note: M4 Pro Mac Miniでのローカルモデルセットアップ は、Appleシリコンによる大規模LLMのローカル実行可能性を示し、日本のスタートアップがエッジAIを検討する際の指標となっている。

**主な議論点**  
コミュニティは、低価格ホームヒューマノイドロボット「Nori」に対し、ハードウェア性能と実用性の間で激論を繰り立てた。RCサーボモーター使用による運動の振 jitter と低精度、力覚フィードバック欠如が問題と指摘され、実環境でのタスク（食器洗いやおもちゃ拾拾）遂行能力に疑問が投げかけられた。また、RPi5の性能不足やWiFi経由の制御遅延懸念、ソフトウェアサブスクリプションモデルに対する不信感（プライバシー・料金・ロックイン）が浮上した。

comments.author: evilmathkid
comments.text: Hi! Author here. Surprised to see this on HN now. Happy to answer any questions! Some context about this: - This is NOT an LLM. its a small ar transformer trained from scratch. One of the points was that extremely complex problems can be tackled without LLMs - Till the v1 of this result, this benchmark was only scaled by LLMs or their finetunes (ofc w enormous training costs). Other attempts performed okayish but used v complex architectures or extremely high amounts of training compute. No one expected a simple AR transformer to perform this well, at this low cost and w these few training samples. - Sample Efficiency is one of the most important unsolved problems today in AI. That's what I was targetting with this work. We know it is easy to increase SE by increasing compute/params, so it was important to constrain cost as much as possible (also why OpenAI's Parameter Golf had fixed compute and why Modded NanoGPT is considered very sample efficient) - Can the perf be improved? Yes but the competition is ongoing so can't talk about it - Personally I think today's frontier models can be beat by training from scratch. Haven't proved this yet tho - Fun: I was new to ML when I posted this first (dec '25). I basically used ARC as a way to learn ML

You should be able to achieve near SoTa with your new method, before you squeeze any lemons. This is, because the old SoTa is typically not using new optimisers and thus your results will be distorted by a large margin. In terms of sample efficiency I want to add two things: Runtime per-puzzle fine tuning is a very good target that provides a LOT of information. People have not looked at evolutionary methods to harness induction since the 90ies - if I was to work on ARC ever again I’m fairly certain this is where I’d look. Best of luck, padawan

comments.author: teraflop
comments.text: The blog post doesn't seem to mention what strikes me as the most interesting application of a model like this, namely extracting semantic information from its latent space. It mentions robotics applications, but only in the context of generating realistic world models for simulation. If you have a robot deployed in an environment, generating synthetic views of the environment you're in doesn't have any obvious value. What does have obvious value is the latent knowledge that the model could have used to generate those synthetic views. For instance, the fact that Atlas is capable of identifying regions of the input images that look like "floors", and smoothly interpolating them and filling in gaps with more floor, suggests that it has a concept of "floor-like walkability" which it's learned from the examples in its training data. And being able to identify the regions of 3D space that correspond to that semantic label would obviously be useful for robot path planning. There's plenty of literature about e.g. using neural networks to estimate walkable areas from a point cloud. And you could imagine just bolting one of those methods to the front of Atlas, using the synthesized point cloud (instead of traditional photogrammetry or LIDAR) as input. But that seems like it's throwing away a lot of potentially useful semantic information, on top of being needlessly inefficient.

comments.text: This is incredible. One potential application that I'm thinking about already is the rapid iteration of video-game map blocking. Being able to drop in some 'initial state' configuration and then have it procedurally generate a handful of alternative configurations could make rapid prototyping a significantly quicker experience, especially if you wanted to see what a potential end result could look like. Furthermore, being able to extract and process world geometry and 3D objects from Atlas could reduce friction in the early stages of indy development, where developer time is stretched thinner. comments.author: kurthr
comments.text: There is also the problem that that impedance mismatch between the gas in the tube and the glass surrounding it is huge so very little power is coupled. Interesting things would be for the tube length/resonance to be closer to the sound frequency of interest (eg 200-2000Hz) and close to critically damped. I have no idea if that's the case. The second question is whether one can simply modify the tube/ballast in a visually imperceptible way. For example, one could insert an IC in the ballast that modulates the power draw of the lamp dependent on the ambient coupled acoustic/vibration power (eg possibly using the lamp as a vibrational microphone). Then pulse modulating the power draw of the lamp at a relatively low noise part of the power spectrum and within the band of the main power transformer filters. The lamps easily draw 40-80W so there's lots of room to work, and there are already Power Factor Correction implementations that use this simple technique to make lamp's inductive loads "look resistive". So what's notable is that either the ballast of the lamp could be tampered with or one of the bulbs. Either one could allow transmission out along power lines, if standard transformers and capacitors are used for power delivery. This is how home powerline ethernet works and it transmits Gb/s rather than the few kb/s needed to get voice out over the power lines. Case in point. I saw a single Korean Samjung lamp interfere with AM radio stations (<1MHz) from 100 meters, by just clipping the power draw of a small fluorescent with a thyristor and oscillator at the ballast of a desk lamp to provide PFC so that thousands of lamps could be placed in huge open plan offices.

comments.author: ivanbakel
comments.text: A very valid take on spec writing. It sometimes feels like the research on formal verification is like the drunkard searching under the lamppost, in that the target is often a domain which is itself well-suited to a particular kind of computer science being done on it. However, I think there is a middle ground between the "naturally verifiable" and the difficult cases. Certain domains, like banking apps, can want correctness guarantees about UI behaviour. A closed-off app can be very normative, so in theory specs like "the user did this action and confirmed it" can be made meaningful. But tying specs to UI is a tricky thing, and it's clearly volatile in a way function boundaries are not - apps go through redesigns, styles and elements move, etc. The abstraction of a UI as a state machine isn't hard to imagine, but actually hooking a spec into the program is a problem unto itself, and the common response is to simply ignore these problematic domains and do something easier like a backend spec that doesn't have to deal with the questions that aren't PL-shaped.

comments.author: nanolith
comments.text: This article comes close to making a fallacious argument about formal methods, which is that formal methods aren't useful unless you can exactly specify how something works. I use model checking (a form of formal methods) daily. I separate the process into three domains: things that must be fully specified, things that can be fully specified, and things that, with the appropriate mitigation, need only have certain properties verified. Most software fits just fine in the latter category. Spend your time on fully verifying process isolation, cryptography, certain core runtime functions / behaviors, and logic relating to authentication and authorization. Everything else can be partially verified, which is much easier. Verify termination, no UB, memory safety, and that function contracts, data structure invariants, and API boundaries are followed. A PDF implementation, a web browser, or a random server application fits cleanly into this decomposition. It matters little if the PDF is rendered oddly, or if the web browser can't interpret a page. But, it matters greatly if these errors could result in a vulnerability that could be exploited, or to a lesser extent, if these errors resulted in the software crashing. Pure formal methods is academic. Apply engineering to this, and you get a real world and practical framework for making software safer.

stories.summary_ja: 記事「Specifications Don't Exist」へのコメントでは、仕様書の有用性と形式手法の適用範囲が主に議論された。UI仕様は頻繁に変更され状態機械として結びつけにくいため、形式検証の対象として不向きだと指摘され、代わりにバックエンドやプロセス隔離、暗号、認証・認可などのコア部分を完全に仕様付けて検証すべきという意見が出た。一方、形式手法は完全仕様が必要だという誤謬に陥りやすく、実際には終了判定やメモリ安全、関数契約などの一部特性を確認すれば十分だとする見方も示された。さらに、LLMで実装から仕様を導出しバグ発見に活用するSpeculaや、仕様を合成可能にする手法が注目され、部分仕様の合成が monolothic 仕様の問題を緩和できるとコメントされている。
stories.editor_note: 仕様は存在しない (2025) は、厳格な仕様書よりも柔軟な合意形成を主張し、日本のソフトウェア開発におけるアジャイル・DevOpsの浸透を裏付ける論調として共有されている。

主な議論点は、求職者が提示する技術スタックと働き方の希望（リモート・オフィス・ハイブリッド、転居可否）に注目が集まったことだ。多くのコメントでは、ロボット／組み込み系（ROS2、Go、Python）やクラウドネイティブ（Rust、Axum、Kubernetes、AWS）など、特定分野の専門性をアピールする姿勢が評価された一方で、フルスタックやバックエンド幅広いスキルを主張する者もおり、専門性と汎用性のどちらが企業に求められるかが議論の焦点になった。  

賛否両論としては、リモート専門を希望する者に対して「タイムゾーンや協調作業のハードルがある」という懸念と、「優秀な人材は場所にとらわれず採用すべき」という支持が分かれた。また、転居不可を明示する姿勢に対して「柔軟性が欠ける」と批判する声と、「生活拠点を固定したいエンジニアのニーズを尊重すべき」という擁護が見られた。  

注目コメントの一つは、オープンソースプロジェクトの維持経験を強調し、「OSSでの実績は信頼性とコミュニティスキルの証明となり、企業内でも同様の協調姿勢が期待できる」と述べ、技術だけでなくコミュニティ貢献度が採用判断に大きく影響するという洞察を示したものだった。

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、このブラウザベースの重力シミュレーターの直感的な操作性と教育的な価値、そしてその実装の軽快さです。コミュニティは、天体の配置や軌道の観察が簡易に行える点を評価し、物理学の基礎を学ぶ上で役立つ可能性に注目しました。特に、重力と運動の法則を視覚的に理解できる点が称賛され、教育現場での活用を期待する声が複数挙げられました。

賛否両論の点としては、シミュレーターの機能の簡素さについての議論があります。一部のユーザーは、より高度な物理法則（例えば相対性理論や量子力学）の連動や、3D視点の実装を希望する声がある一方で、簡潔さが逆に初心者には優しさを提供するという前向きな意見も見られました。また、パフォーマンスについて、大規模な天体配置時に重い負荷がかかるという報告と、ブラウザの種類による違いが指摘され了一些。

注目コメントとして、既存の類似ツールと比較した洞察のあるコメントが挙げられます。あるコメントは、このアプリが「Newton's Playground」という既存のソフトウェアと類似しているが、ブラウザ内での実行という点でより Accessible である点を強調しました。他のコメントでは、開発者に対して、軌道の安定性を高めるアルゴリズムの改善や、ファイルからのデータ読み込み機能の追加を要望するなど、技術的な詳細に言及した建設的なフィードバックがなされていました。全体的に、community はこのプロジェクトを楽しく、教育的に価値があるものと認識し、今後の発展に期待を寄せる姿勢がうかがえました。
